sections.b: 4 Maccabees retells the deaths of 2 Maccabees 7 at three times the length, brother by brother (4 Maccabees 8:1-12:20). The tortures and their order change (the fourth, not the first, loses his tongue; the youngest throws himself onto the griddles), and two things are missing: the brothers never confess sins of their own, as two of them do in 2 Maccabees (2 Maccabees 7:18, 32), and they say nothing about the body rising again. What they say instead is that the tyrant can touch only the body (4 Maccabees 10:4), that they will "carry off the prizes of virtue" (4 Maccabees 9:8), and that the king faces eternal fire. Brother after brother is offered release for one bite (the fifth comes forward without waiting to be asked, 4 Maccabees 11:1-3), and every one refuses, which may be the picture behind "would not take the release they were offered" (Hebrews 11:35).

sections.h: Aaron and the angel of fire (4 Maccabees 7:11)
sections.b: 4 Maccabees compares the old priest Eleazar to Aaron in Numbers 16, who ran with his censer into the crowd "and made atonement for the people" (Numbers 16:47). Numbers names no angel; the Wisdom of Solomon speaks of "the destroyer" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:25), and 4 Maccabees of "the angel who was burning them", whom Aaron defeated. The comparison sets up Eleazar's death as a priest's act for the nation (4 Maccabees 6:28-29).
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 7:11-12; Numbers 16:41-50; Wisdom of Solomon 18:20-25; 4 Maccabees 6:28-29

sections.b: 4 Maccabees reads Isaac as a willing victim and makes him a model for the martyrs: old Eleazar overcomes the rack "with a reason like Isaac's" (4 Maccabees 7:14), the brothers remind each other that Isaac endured to be slaughtered at his father's hand (4 Maccabees 13:12), and the mother recalls Abraham's haste (4 Maccabees 16:20). Genesis itself gives Isaac only one question (Genesis 22:7).

4 Maccabees says that those wholly devoted to godliness "do not die to God" but, like Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, "live to God" (4 Maccabees 7:19; 4 Maccabees 16:25). Jesus argued from the same three names that God "is not God of dead people but of living ones, for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38). Jesus uses the point to prove the resurrection; 4 Maccabees uses it of the soul's life with God at death.

sections.h: The soul out of the torturer's reach (4 Maccabees 9-10)
sections.b: The brothers of 4 Maccabees speak of the soul as the self that torture cannot reach: "You will not touch my soul, not even if you want to" (4 Maccabees 10:4). The first brother "broke off his life" at death (4 Maccabees 9:25), in Greek "broke off his soul", as if it snapped loose from the body. The book's hope is the soul's life with God, with no word of the body rising, which sets it beside the Wisdom of Solomon ("no torment will touch them at all", Wisdom of Solomon 3:1) and apart from 2 Maccabees 7. Even a Roman noticed the belief: Jews "think the souls of those killed in battle or by execution are eternal" (Histories of Tacitus 5:5).
sections.refs: 4 Maccabees 9:7; 4 Maccabees 9:25; 4 Maccabees 10:4; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1; Matthew 10:28; Histories of Tacitus 5:5

sections.h: The martyrs without the resurrection (4 Maccabees)
sections.b: In 2 Maccabees the brothers die hoping that "the King of the world will raise us" (2 Maccabees 7:9). Retelling the same deaths, 4 Maccabees leaves resurrection out. The brothers expect "the prizes of virtue", life with the patriarchs, and "incorruption" (4 Maccabees 9:8; 4 Maccabees 9:22), and say the soul cannot be touched (4 Maccabees 10:4). R. B. Townshend (1913) concluded: "Apparently there is no resurrection of the body" in the book.

4 Maccabees borrows the Stoics' language: only the wise and self-restrained man is the brave lord of the passions (4 Maccabees 7:23), and those whose reason is weak are ruled by them (4 Maccabees 7:20). But it changes the content. The Stoics held that the virtuous person feels no passions; this book says reason is not their uprooter but their opponent (4 Maccabees 3:5), and its wise man is the one who trusts God and keeps the law (4 Maccabees 7:21-22).

sections.h: Eternal fire for the tyrant (4 Maccabees 9-12)
sections.b: Each brother in 4 Maccabees promises the king fire: "an eternal torture by fire" (4 Maccabees 9:9), "tortures that never end" (4 Maccabees 10:11), "a fiercer and eternal fire" that will not let him go for all eternity (4 Maccabees 12:12). The book does not use the name Gehenna, but its picture is the one Jesus uses, "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48), taken from Isaiah 66:24.

In 4 Maccabees the youngest of the seven, once untied, "threw himself down onto the griddles" (4 Maccabees 12:20), and the mother later throws herself into the fire (4 Maccabees 17:1); in 2 Maccabees both are killed by the king. Jewish tradition honored those who chose death rather than be forced into sin (Bavli Gittin 57b). R. B. Townshend (1913) notes that John Chrysostom praised the boy's leap as a leap into a font of baptism. Augustine denied that any canonical book permits suicide, but would not condemn the women martyrs who drowned themselves to escape rape, allowing that they may have acted by divine prompting, as Samson did (City of God 1.20, 1.26).

Antiochus offers the seven brothers high office if they give up "the ancestral rule of your way of life" and "take part in Greek life" (4 Maccabees 8:7-8), finishing the work 2 Maccabees credits to Jason, who "moved his own people over to the Greek stamp" (2 Maccabees 4:10). Yet the speaker himself uses Greek philosophy and the games freely: the brothers' training ground is their torture (4 Maccabees 11:20), a different gymnasium from Jason's (4 Maccabees 4:20).

The test in 4 Maccabees is a single bite of pork, offered to each brother with the promise of release (4 Maccabees 8:2; 4 Maccabees 9:16; 4 Maccabees 11:13). The sixth brother sums up his crime: refusing to "eat defiling food" (4 Maccabees 11:16). Later Jewish law allowed most commandments to be broken to save a life, but ruled that "in a time of religious persecution" even a minor commandment must not be broken under threat (Bavli Sanhedrin 74a), the situation of the seven.

sections.h: A tongue that sang hymns (4 Maccabees 10:17-21)
sections.b: When Antiochus orders the fourth brother's tongue cut out, the boy answers that "God hears the silent too", and that the king is cutting out "a tongue that sang hymns to God" (4 Maccabees 10:18, 21). Hannah prayed when "no one could hear her voice" (1 Samuel 1:13), and the psalmists promise to praise God with the tongue (Psalm 35:28).

Hebrews remembers sufferers who "would not take the release they were offered, so that they could win a better resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). In 4 Maccabees each of the seven brothers is offered release if he will eat (4 Maccabees 8:2; 4 Maccabees 9:16; 4 Maccabees 11:13), and each refuses. Hebrews' hope of resurrection is the hope of 2 Maccabees 7, not of 4 Maccabees, so the martyrs of Hebrews 11:35 are the same people as in both books, but the wording of the hope belongs to 2 Maccabees.
